en: The Heart Sutra Explained by Xuelang; Narrated by Hong'en.

This *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* is the World-Honored One manifesting the Dharma through the person. By clearly perceiving the emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha*), he elucidates the profoundly deep *prajñā*.
Furthermore, fearing that people might not understand, he explains it himself, saying: "To perceive that the five aggregates are all empty is to transcend all suffering and calamity.
What is meant by the emptiness of the aggregates? It is because form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form;

and as for sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, none of them are not empty. Fearing that people might not know the purport of "form is itself emptiness," he explains it once more.

It is said: These dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness. Within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), that which arises is fundamentally non-arising, and that which ceases is originally without cessation.

As for being neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing—since these are the characteristics of emptiness, although they possess the various dharmas of the five aggregates, they are fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, increase and decrease;
thus it is clear that there is no form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Thus, one clearly perceives that the five aggregates are all empty. Since the five aggregates are empty, then the three—sense bases, sense objects, and consciousnesses—of the mundane world;
the four truths and twelve links of dependent origination of the supramundane; and even the subject that realizes and the object realized, are all without exception empty.
Once the mundane aggregates and elements no longer exist, there is likewise no supramundane wisdom or attainment. When both subject and object are forgotten, how could the five aggregates exist?
Therefore, when there is absolutely nothing to be apprehended, it is only then called "profound Prajñā. Bodhisattvas rely upon this, whereby their minds are without hindrance;
they are free from fear and far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, and are able to reach ultimate Nirvāṇa. All Buddhas of the three periods of time rely upon this.
Thus, Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi can be attained; the fetters of the five abodes are exhausted, and the two types of death are both forgotten.

What suffering, affliction, or calamity would there not be delivered from? All this is possible because one perceives the emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha-śūnyatā*). Therefore, it is praised as follows:
"This emptiness of the aggregates is the profound Prajñā, the Great Illuminating Mantra, the Divine Mantra," for it is capable of transforming the ordinary person into a sage.
If one were to spell out this incantation word-for-word, fearing that people might not believe it, [the scripture] further states: "It can eliminate all suffering;

it is true and not false. It subsequently recites the secret mantra to cause one to sever speech and still discursive thought, thereby realizing the *prajñā* of the emptiness of these aggregates (*skandha*).
This means that by merely departing from deluded conditions, one is immediately the Tathāgata of Suchness; this is Avalokiteśvara.

One is able to practice this alone; therefore, it is called "mastery" (*vaśitā*). Even with the six hundred fascicles of the Great Sūtra, one takes this as the core, just as a person has a heart that serves as the master of the body. How simple, direct, and clear this is!

Yet those in the world who are mere peddlers of words boast and advertise themselves, falsely discoursing on *prajñā*, recklessly producing forced interpretations, and dragging [the teaching] into confusion.
The spreading branches and trailing vines obstruct right knowledge and vision. One blind man leads the way in front, and a hundred blind men follow and harmonize with him behind;

they blind the eyes of others, needlessly increasing the suffering of karma. Out of compassion for the ignorant younger generation—for whom these creeping weeds are difficult to eradicate and whose lamp of the Buddha is about to go out—I have, against my own will, recorded this brief summary of the essential meaning of the beginning and end of the sutra as follows.
I await one who understands words. It is much like raising one's voice to stop an echo. Is it possible for me to wish for no words?
Thus ends the *Heart Sūtra*.
